Which credentials were on a machine, and when: the entries to rotate, only those whose exposed value is still live, and one command that rotates exactly them. --host NODE asks the hub; --host local reads this machine's materialisation log

Categories (the flat, slash-nested tags in the sidebar)

Read a CXF file. Every item is appended as one or more new entries: see vault_core::cxf's module doc for the one-credential-vs-several (bundle) rule and why this is append-only rather than merge-aware
Write a synthetic vault with invented values into an empty directory, for bug reports. Needs no password; the vault's own password is printed
Print the machine-readable contract: commands, flags, exit codes, schemas
Compare two entries field by field. Secrets show as fingerprints unless --reveal, so equal and different are answerable without reading either

List entries missing metadata fields (exit 10 when any are)
List entries (same filters as unv list)

Restore a previous value by its position in entry history

Record a rotation, optionally storing the new secret
Change fields on an existing entry
Add or remove tags
Show secret-free lifecycle events and credential generations
Record that a stored browser session still works
Resolve a project's env_file chunks into a deployable .env (${refs} resolved)
Run a command with secrets in its environment: they never reach stdout
Export vault entries
Write a file-shaped credential to disk, and print the variable that names it
Write the credential to disk and print the .env line that names it
Generators: secrets, passwords, certificates, SSH keys
A self-signed certificate and its private key
A password from the selected character sets
A passphrase of random words (11 bits of entropy per word)
Random bytes as hex / base64 / base64url
List entropy sources and whether each one works on this machine
An ed25519 SSH keypair
Print full details of a single entry
What a term in the product means: a field, setting, secret type, concept, command or flag.

Check text on stdin against the exact values this vault holds, before it is pasted into a chat or an agent prompt. Prints the entry and field names found, never a value; exits 10 when a value of eight or more characters is in the text
Does the text on stdin hold a value this vault holds? (names only, no network call)
Serve the browser paste guard over native messaging on stdin and stdout (the browser starts it)
Register the native messaging host with a browser so its paste guard extension can reach this vault
The config time machine: a snapshot of every rendered config whenever a save changes it, diffable, verifiable and pruned by policy. Stdout shows secrets as fingerprints; --reveal or --out shows them
Unified diff between two snapshots of one config; by default the newest two. A rotated secret shows as a changed fingerprint

Compare a stored snapshot with a file on this machine - typically a node's live config fetched with unv node pull. Without --reveal only the names of the differing lines are shown, never what follows them
List snapshots, newest first. Shows names, times and hashes, never content
Show or change the retention policy and whether history is on
Delete snapshots that are both beyond the newest --keep and older than --days, leaving a checkpoint. Deletes the only record of what was deployed then
Show one snapshot. Fingerprinted unless --reveal; --out FILE writes the real file (0600)
Record a snapshot of every config that changed, now
Snapshot count, size and oldest
Recompute every hash and chain and check each checkpoint against the audit chain
Which snapshot a file's SHA-256 came from (e.g. the hash a node reports)
Import entries from a .env file (creates/updates env_var entries)
Import from a secrets service: OpenBao, Infisical, Bitwarden Secrets Manager or AWS
Import from another password manager or a Nextcloud config.php
List vault entries (table view)
Authenticate once and cache the session (remote servers)
Forget cached sessions
Losslessly plan and import a local configuration file
Save imported entries, source identity and encrypted archives together
List or export encrypted, preserved source material
Write one encrypted archive record to a user-selected private file
Make this vault the authority for the entries a Git-store import (SOPS, pass, gopass) created
Compare a Git source, as it is now, with what was last imported. Read-only on both sides
Find secrets left in plain text under a folder, with your own gitleaks, and offer them as migration candidates
Inspect a source without changing the vault
List migration summaries without source values or file contents
Refresh the vault from the source this migration read, one way. Preview unless --apply
Hand authority back to the source. Refused when a credential changed after cutover
Re-render a template migration and compare its SHA-256 with its source

Nodes: agents on other hosts that observe, and when told to apply, config files rendered from this vault. token, ls, show, revoke, pull and accept manage them on a hub (unv-server --nodes); enroll, run and check run on the managed host
Record a pull target's current file as accepted into the vault, so it reads in_sync until it changes again
Pushes waiting for a human, with --all the decided ones too

Approve one held push. Shows the diff against what the node has and the hash being approved first (secrets as fingerprints unless --reveal); --yes skips the question for someone who has looked. The approval is for those exact bytes and lapses in an hour
Approver devices: the key on this machine whose signature a node set to device approval (and configured with approver = "…") accepts as yours
Devices the hub accepts
Tell the hub this machine's key counts as your approval (hub, owner only)
Stop accepting a device, by (at least 8 characters of) its fingerprint
This machine's approver public key and fingerprint (the key is made on first use, 0600). Put the public key in a node's config as approver
Show the hub's automation public key for a node's automation_approver
Validate a node config and show what it would report. Contacts no one
On the managed host: spend an enrollment token and save this node's identity. Nothing is read from the vault

On the managed host, as root: install the agent as a hardened systemd service (a launchd job on macOS), enrol it, and give it access to exactly the files you name. --plan prints every step without running any
List enrolled nodes and each target's status (hub)
On the managed host: ask to be paired with a hub that opens no port (the desktop app). Makes this node's identity and certificate and prints a request for the hub's owner
Hub (owner): enrol a listening node from its pairing request, without a token
On the managed host: finish pairing with the reply the hub's owner got back
Hold every push to a node for a human (required), or stop (none)
Fetch a pull target's file from the node. Written with --out (0600); there is no stdout form, because the file is the node's own and holds its secrets
Reject one held push; the same bytes are not asked about again
Stop a node receiving config. Files already written stay where they are
On the managed host: beat to the hub and carry out what this node's own config allows. Runs until stopped. A node enrolled with --listen waits for the hub to dial it instead
One node in full: key fingerprint, host, and every target (hub)
Mint a single-use enrollment token for a new node (hub, owner only)
The token is a one-time credential: written to --out (0600), or printed only with --reveal

Show the read/write expressions for a user or class

Allow a plugin to be called, after showing what it declares

List the cached sessions: which servers, which users, which is default
Run a command while replacing known vault values in its text output
Serve the Ed25519 keys in this vault over the OpenSSH agent protocol, so ssh can sign with a key that never sits under ~/.ssh. Signing only: it never returns a private key. Unix only
Where this CLI is pointed and what the vault holds
Support: a small, readable file for a bug report
Versions, counts and check results of the local vault: no values, names, paths or hosts
List every tag in the vault with its entry count
Entry presets for common services: list them or show what one pre-fills
List the presets
Show what a preset pre-fills and which fields it expects
Guided add: attach a seed to an existing entry (matched by exact provider name) or create a bare password-typed one with an empty primary. Mirrors the desktop Authenticator panel's "Add 2FA" form
Advance a counter-based (HOTP) seed to its next position
Print the current code for an entry
Write every stored seed in a format another authenticator reads
Import seeds from another authenticator app's export
List the entries that carry a seed. Names and parameters, never codes
Forget an entry's seed. The old value stays in entry history
Write the otpauth:// URI, for enrolling a replacement phone
The unique-ID registry. Server-side only: refused against a local vault with no --server
Advisory only: "unique right now". register/mint are the operations that actually reserve a value
One value → issued/unknown plus the metadata the caller may see
Generate in-process, check, retry up to 3 times on collision, register, and return the value that was actually stored
Delete registry rows before a date. **Deletes the only evidence an ID was issued**: a pruned ID can be issued again undetected. Dry-run first
Record values minted elsewhere. Fails closed per value on a collision: nothing else in the batch is rolled back
Row count, size on disk, oldest entry
Update this executable from a signed release (standalone archives only)
Say whether a newer signed release exists. Installs nothing
Download, verify and install the newer release over this executable
Publisher: build and sign the manifest for a release's archives
Pin a project and environment to this directory (writes .unv.json)
Create a user. Prompts for a password unless --no-password
Assign a class, or remove the current one with --none
Set or clear a user's password
Require a write to match EVERY scope, not any one of them
API tokens for a user
Mint a token. Write it to a file with --out so it never reaches stdout
Second factor (TOTP) for a sub-user
Phase two: prove the authenticator works, which enables the factor
Remove the factor and destroy the secret
Phase one: mint a secret. Does **not** enable the factor
Show whether a user is enrolled and whether the factor is enabled
Which instance of the vault this is, and making a restored one the live one
Make this instance the live one (asks first; the old instance must be retired)
Change the master password (re-encrypts the vault; asks first)
Show the vault id, the instance id, its epoch and role
Watch a .env file for changes and sync into the vault
Show which identity this CLI would use, and whether its session still works
A person's confirmation, tied to the exact bytes they saw, that a node may apply a change. An automation cannot satisfy a human approval.
The password-hashing function that turns the master password and the salt into the vault key, with 64 MiB of memory, 3 passes and 1 lane.
An append-only record of actions on the vault. Its rows are chained by hashes, and unv audit --verify checks the chain.
Which credentials were on a machine, and when: the entries to rotate if that machine is compromised, and only those whose exposed value is still live.
A local socket from the unlocked desktop app that lets unv read the entries flagged for local scripts. It is off by default and read-only.
A decoy credential planted where a thief would look first. Using it records an alert in the audit log, so a theft is noticed after the fact; it prevents nothing.
A flat label for grouping entries, listed in the sidebar's Categories section. Category names nest by writing a slash. It is separate from tags and projects.
Remembering a server certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint and refusing to talk to a server that presents a different one. It is never re-pinned silently.
A piece of configuration kept with a project, such as a service's file, that can refer to entries by name and is rendered with their values filled in.
A snapshot of every rendered configuration taken whenever a save changes it, which can be compared, verified and pruned. The command-line view hides secrets as fingerprints.
One secret record in the vault: a provider name, a value and its metadata. An entry is identified by its id, never by its position in a list.
The rule that turns an entry into a variable name: an optional prefix, the provider, the key id, the version, the label and the role, joined with underscores, for example SPOTIFY_V2_GAME_ID.
unv exec runs a command with secrets in its environment so they never reach standard output.
A short SHA-256 digest and a length shown in place of a secret, so two values can be told apart or compared without printing either.
A numbered version of a credential's value, with a fingerprint, where it came from and when it was active or revoked. Replacing a secret's value starts a new generation.
A record in which each row includes the hash of the row before it, so an edited or deleted row is detectable.
A check of the vault for weak, expiring, duplicated and stale-reference secrets and for recovery code sets that are nearly used up.
The side that proposes changes to nodes: unv-server with nodes enabled, or the desktop app while it is unlocked. A hub only proposes; the node's own configuration decides what is written.
A recorded fact in an entry's timeline, such as a cutover or a deployment, kept with its time and source.
The vault lives on your own machine as one encrypted file and works without any server. A server is optional and is for sharing and remote access.

The password that opens the vault. The vault key is derived from it with Argon2id and a random salt and is never written to disk. There is no recovery service, so a forgotten master password cannot be recovered.
A bounded local record of which secrets reached this machine through exec, --out, --reveal or the desktop's clipboard copies. It holds fingerprints, never values, and is kept outside the audit chain.
An agent on another host that observes configuration files and, when told to, applies files rendered from the vault.
A check that matches pasted text against the exact values in the vault so a secret is not pasted into an AI chat. It runs on your computer and reports entry names, never values.
A program that adds destinations, notifiers or issuers to unv through a small line-based protocol. It runs with a cleared environment and time limits.
A group of entries and configuration chunks shown in the sidebar. Every entry belongs to the catch-all Universal project and can belong to others. Projects nest by writing a slash in the name.
An encrypted file for restoring the vault on a new machine, made and checked with unv recover.
Printing a secret as a fingerprint and a length instead of its value. It is on by default and fails closed: a field prints only if it is listed as public.
A placeholder such as ${GitHub} or ${GitHub/username} that is replaced by an entry's value when copying, exporting or rendering. A name that matches more than one entry is refused, not guessed.
A vault served by unv-server and reached over HTTPS, where the client pins the server's certificate and never silently re-pins it.
Showing or printing the real value of a secret, with the eye button or --reveal. Without it values are redacted.
Replacing a credential at its issuer: the new one is stored first and the old one is revoked last, and only when that is safe.
Sixteen random bytes in vault.salt, written once and used with the password to derive the key. Nothing can recompute it, so a vault whose salt is lost cannot be opened.

An opt-in mode of unv exec on Linux that runs the command in a bubblewrap sandbox: read-only file system, empty home, runtime and vault directories, and no network. It refuses to run where it cannot be enforced.
Which kind of secret an entry is, such as an API key, a password, a certificate or a Wi-Fi network. The type decides which fields and form layout apply.
The encrypted version of SQLite that the vault is stored in.
A local socket that serves SSH keys from the vault to the ssh program and records each signing in the audit log.
The state of a restored vault copy. It can be opened, read, verified and exported, but it does not push to nodes or run scheduled operations until it is made the live copy.
The catch-all project that every entry belongs to.
The UnENVerse command-line program.
The optional UnENVerse server: it serves a vault over HTTPS with users, tokens and permissions.
The encrypted SQLCipher database, vault.db with its vault.salt, that holds all entries, projects and settings. It is opened with the master password.
ok
error: unclassified failure
invalid: well-formed request, invalid input
released: unv exec refused: the secret may only be released to other commands
usage: bad arguments (clap)
not_found: no such entry, project, chunk, user or class
ambiguous: the name matched several things; error.details.candidates lists them
denied: authentication failed or the session lacks the permission
conflict: already exists, or a concurrent write won
unavailable: vault or server unreachable, or locked
needs_confirmation: destructive command without --yes on a non-tty
redacted: output would contain secrets; use --out or --reveal
How much the credential allows at the issuer: read, write, admin or custom. It is filled in from the issuer's key prefix by enrich and is never enforced.
An optional name that tells apart several accounts you hold with the same provider, for example a personal account and a work account.

Who the credential acts as when it is used: anonymous, a user, a service, a bot, an app installation or an admin. It is one of the axes describing an API key, filled in from the key's issuer prefix by enrich, and it is never enforced.
A short description of what the key is used for.
The primary secret of an entry: an API key, a password, a variable's value, or whatever the entry's type treats as its main value. It is printed redacted unless you reveal it.

A second secret kept beside an API key, such as a client secret or a shared secret. Only the api_key type uses it. A new entry keeps such extra secrets as additional values instead, and the field stays for entries that already hold one.
The base URL of the service's API. The form relabels this field by type, for example Login URL for a password and Site URL for a certificate.
The app you built or run that uses this secret. It is separate from Purpose, which is what you told the issuer.
The organisation that owns the app this secret was made for, or its account with the issuer.
What that app does with this secret.

Where the app this secret was made for lives: its homepage or console. It is separate from the sites the secret is used on and from the issuer's API URL. It must be an http or https address with no user name or password in it, and only such an address is shown as a link.
The version of the app that uses this secret. The API or SDK version the key was issued for is a separate field.
Descriptors of files attached to an entry. The bytes and locators are redacted unless you reveal.

The header or query-parameter name that the Sent as setting puts the value in. It defaults to X-Api-Key for a named header and to api_key for a query parameter, and it means nothing for bearer and basic, whose shapes are fixed.

How a credential is sent in a request: as a bearer token, as basic authentication, in a named header, or in a query parameter. It turns a stored string into a working request, which two entries that look identical can need in completely different ways.
For a named header, the value that is sent, with {key} standing for the credential. Empty sends the credential on its own.
Who owns the credential and under which account. The fields that locate the account are redacted in command-line output.

The contents of a file-shaped credential, such as a service-account JSON, an Apple .p8 file, an mTLS bundle or a kubeconfig. These are used by pointing a program at a file, so the vault stores the contents here and the mount path says where to write them. The size is capped, because storing a truncated credential silently would be worse than refusing it.
The file-system path or reference of a credential file. Entries of the file_blob type only.

The id of the bundle entry this entry belongs to. Membership is stored once, on the member, the same way a pool is, so an older build that deletes the bundle cannot leave two disagreeing copies of it. Empty means the entry is not in a bundle.
A sort key that places a member within its bundle. It has gaps and is never an identity: nothing refers to an entry by its position.
On a bundle entry, the id of the member that the card's main Copy button copies. Empty means nothing can be copied from the collapsed card yet.
A member's own name inside its bundle, such as discord, web or v3. It is unique within the bundle and is how templates address the member, as ${bundle:Name/slot} or {slot.field}.
The callback URL of an OAuth or webhook service.
The category tags an entry carries. They are listed in the sidebar's Categories section and can be used as a scope when giving a user access.
The authority that issued the certificate, for example Let's Encrypt or Google. Certificate entries only.
The private key, in PEM form, that pairs with the entry's certificate.
The certificate content in PEM form, as the full chain. Certificate entries only.
What kind of thing a composite template is. It decides how values are encoded into the template and whether an Open action is offered.
The shape of a composite entry's rendered value with its holes left in. It is printed as it is and not masked, because it holds the holes and not the values.
Marks a credential as known to be leaked and in need of rotation at once. It shows up as a critical item in the health scan.
Where to revoke or rotate this credential.

When the entry was first written to the vault, as an ISO-8601 time. It is never rewritten on edit, and it is a creation date, not a modification date. Entries from before the field existed get a date inferred from the vault's own records, or none, and then show as unknown.
The Simple Icons name to use as the provider's icon. Empty means the icon is detected automatically.
Longer free-text notes about an entry.
Notes to yourself about an entry: extra metadata or usage notes. It is separate from the description of what the key is for.
The email address associated with this credential. It is a separate field from the username and from the account name.

Environment-variable prefixes that the services consuming this credential add. For a key, the prefixes ND and SPOTIFYD mean that Navidrome reads it as ND_LASTFM_APIKEY. For a chunk, the first prefix is the chunk's environment namespace, for example AM for AM_JWT_SECRET.
A hint about what kind of value an env_var entry holds, used for display and filtering.
The deployment context this credential belongs to.
When the credential expires, as an ISO-8601 date, or empty if it never does. Credentials close to expiry are listed by the health scan and by unv rotate-check.

How safe it is to expose the value: publishable, server only, or verify only. It suggests whether the primary value may be printed but never sets it, so a wrongly detected prefix cannot make redaction print less.
Extra named fields beyond the fixed ones, for example db, port and host for a database entry. Each has a name and a value, and a value can be marked public so that it prints.

How a derived header is built for a web session, for example the *arr family's X-Api-Key, YouTube's SAPISIDHASH or LinkedIn's csrf header copied off a cookie. A derived header is computed when you copy it, so a copied header is only good briefly, and the interface says so.

The entry's stable unique identifier, assigned once when it is created and never changed. It is the entry's identity wherever that must survive edits and reordering: version history, audit rows, access scoping and which cards are expanded. A vault from before the field existed gets a UUID filled in.
The IP addresses the issuer allows this credential to be used from, kept here as a record.
When the issuer created the credential. If it is not known it stays empty instead of being invented.
How precisely the issued-at time is known: exact, date, month, year or unknown. Old vaults use unknown.
Where the issuer runs: a hosted service (saas), your own server (self hosted) or your own machine (local). Filled in by enrich.
Tells apart two credentials from the same provider. It is part of the entry's identity: it is what ${Provider_KeyId} addresses and what access scoping matches.
A short token inserted into generated variable names after the version, as in SPOTIFY_V2_GAME_ID. It is not the account name, because account names are often email addresses.

The variable name this entry was last copied or exported under. It is kept because renaming a provider, version or label silently renames every variable the entry generates, while a .env already on a server keeps the old name.
When the credential was last rotated by hand, set with Mark as rotated, as an ISO-8601 time.

When you last confirmed that a web session credential still works. A session cannot be rotated, because rotating it means logging in again in a browser, so this date is what its health check uses instead.
Whether this entry may be served to local scripts through the unlocked desktop app. It is off by default and is set per entry.

Where the program that uses this credential expects to find it as a file. A service-account JSON, an Apple .p8 file and a kubeconfig are used by pointing at them, so the variable names the path and never the contents, and unv file write puts the file there.
When true, the entry floats to the top of every filtered view.
Data specific to a plugin or adapter. It is treated as secret and redacted unless you reveal it.

The name of the key pool this entry belongs to, empty for a standalone key. Entries that share a pool name are interchangeable credentials for the same service, so a caller can swap to another when one is rate limited. Membership is explicit: two keys for one provider do not pool automatically. The swap state is kept per machine, not in the vault.
The billing model of the service the credential is for: free, local, paid or conditional.
Marks the primary value as safe to print, such as an OAuth client id, a Stripe pk_ key or an AWS access key id. It opts the value out of redaction everywhere.

What the primary value is. It becomes the last segment of its generated variable name, so a client id exports as SPOTIFY_ID rather than SPOTIFY. A new entry starts with its type name here, which gives GITHUB_API_KEY, and a blank role keeps the bare name that every already deployed .env uses.
The ids of the projects an entry belongs to. It always contains Universal, the catch-all every entry carries, and a grant for a specific project is never satisfied by it.
Where an entry came from when it was imported or migrated. The fields that locate the source are redacted in command-line output.

The name of the service or thing the secret belongs to, such as GitHub or DATABASE_URL. Every entry has one. It is the name you see and the name references use, and it can be shared by several entries told apart by their key ids.

What the credential was requested for: the justification given to the issuer on the application form. It is separate from the API description (what the key is) and from details (notes to yourself). It is worth writing down when you write it, because months later nobody remembers.

A human-readable description of the rate limit, such as 100 req/min. It is the older form: the count and period fields are what the interface and the health scan read, and this text is still written so an older build can read the entry.
The rate limit as a number, paired with the period. Empty means not known, which is not the same as zero. A count without a period is meaningless and is dropped when read.
What the old free-text rate limit said when it could not be read as a count and a period, such as varies by endpoint. It is kept because the person who wrote it knew something the fields cannot say.
The window the rate limit count applies to: second, minute, hour, day, week, month or year.
What the credential can reach: public data, your own account, an organisation, the local network, billing or infrastructure. It is filled in by enrich and never enforced.
How often the credential should be rotated, in days. When it is set, the health scan flags the entry once it is overdue since it was last rotated.
The OAuth scopes or permission strings granted to this credential.
The same as primary public, for the API secret. It is rare, but an issuer's secret is sometimes public.
What the API secret is called when the default SECRET is wrong, for example an Auth Token for Twilio or a private key for Apple. It becomes the last segment of the secret's generated variable name.
The stored name of the secret type of an entry. It decides which type-specific fields and form layout apply.

The localStorage and sessionStorage values a web session needs beside its cookies. A storage token is as much a live credential as the cookies next to it, so it never appears in basic metadata or in redacted output.
Free-form labels for quick cross-cutting grouping, separate from categories and projects.
The HMAC the issuer uses to generate codes. Absent means SHA-1, which is what almost every issuer uses. It is written only when the issuer said something else.
The next counter an HOTP seed will use. It is written whenever the seed is counter-based, and zero is a real position. It is state rather than configuration, so advancing it is an explicit action.
The number of digits in the generated code. Absent means 6.
What the seed is: totp (time-based, the default when absent), hotp (counter-based) or steam (Steam Guard's five-character codes).
The number of seconds a code is valid for. Absent means 30.

The authenticator seed a service issued you, in base32. UnENVerse generates from it the code you type into that service's login. Pasting the whole otpauth:// address fills in the algorithm, digits and period. It is separate from the second factor on UnENVerse's own user logins.

The User-Agent a web session was created with. Replaying a session cookie without the matching User-Agent usually fails, so it is half of the credential. It is also a fingerprint, so it never appears in basic metadata.

A value built from a template with holes in it, such as a calendar URL with a mailbox id and a key inside. The pieces are stored as extra values and the rendered value is shown from the template.
A connection string for a database or service, such as postgresql://user:pass@host/db, kept as one value.
A logged-in web session: its cookie jar, the storage tokens it needs and the User-Agent it was made with. The interface calls it Web session; the type id is still cookie.
A cryptocurrency wallet's recovery phrase. The health scan checks it against the BIP39 word list and reports a bad checksum, without printing it.
The access details of a database: host, port, database name, user and password as named values.
An environment variable, or a set of named variables, as a .env file would hold them. The values are kept as named extra values.
A credential that is a file, such as a service-account JSON, an Apple .p8 or a kubeconfig. The vault stores its contents and a mount path says where it is written.
A GPG key: its public key, its public identifiers and its expiry date, which can be filled in by pasting the public key.
A record of an identity document such as a passport, kept as named values.
A software or product license key.
A service on your own machine or network, such as Sonarr, kept with its address and the way its key is sent.
An OAuth client: its client id and secret, with a refresh token that unv oauth refresh can exchange for a new access token.
A passkey stored for import and export, so it can move between password managers. It is not what unlocks this vault.
A login password for a website or service, kept with the login URL and, optionally, a username and an email address.
A set of single-use backup codes for an account. A used code stays in the list marked USED with its date, and reading a code never uses it up. The health scan warns when two or fewer codes are left.
A token for a package registry such as npm, kept with the registry's URL.
A free-text note with no single secret value, kept encrypted like everything else in the vault.
A phrase a site asks for beside the password and the two-factor code, such as a memorable phrase or a security answer.
A key used to sign things, such as webhooks or tokens. The URL where its public keys can be verified can be recorded with it.
An SSH private key in OpenSSH form for a host or service. The SSH agent can serve an unencrypted Ed25519 key from the vault.
An account on a private tracker: the passkey or announce URL that identifies you to it.
A Usenet provider: its server address and your login.
A Wi-Fi network: its name (SSID), passphrase and security type. The Copy menu can produce a Wi-Fi QR string.
The hex colour used for highlights and active states.
The top-level panel currently open: secrets, tools, users, remote or authenticator.
The id of the tool pane currently open.
Which side of the window the activity bar is on: left or right.
Whether the activity bar shows icons only or icons with labels.
Whether the Authenticator screen also shows the code that comes next. It is off by default, because the next code is a second working credential that lives longer than the one on screen.
The number of minutes of inactivity before the vault locks itself.
How dense the secret cards in the grid are: compact, medium or large.
The number of seconds after an in-app copy before the desktop app empties the clipboard, only if the clipboard still holds what the app copied. 0 means never.
The sidebar sections that are currently folded shut in the secrets sidebar.
The sidebar tree nodes you folded shut, written as p: followed by a project id or c: followed by a category name.
When on, the config check resolves an nginx proxy_pass host against the services of every project, the same as unv check --all-projects.

How much of an entry a copy produces: basic, extended or full. It is a default and not a limit: the copy button's menu offers the others and Value only on every card, and a one-off choice there is not saved as the new default.
How precisely a key's created time is shown in the timeline: date, minute or second. Stored values always carry seconds.
A string of CSS added after all the built-in styles.
The value filled into the Account field when you add a new secret.
The format used by Copy All and by the single-entry copy button on cards: dotenv, yaml or json.
The providers, case-folded, whose prompt to bundle them was dismissed.
Where the interface's generators draw randomness from: os, or file:PATH.
The case of a generated environment-variable name: upper, lower or preserve. Upper is the shell convention and what every exporter has always produced, so lower is offered and not assumed.
Which entry field is used as the value when copying for a .env: the API key, the API secret or the key id.

When on, the entry's first consumer prefix is put in front of generated names, so ND_SPOTIFY_ID rather than SPOTIFY_ID. It is off by default because a prefix belongs to one consumer of a credential, and turning it on renames every variable the vault generates.

Offers the untested project types (Kubernetes, SSH config, Traefik, Apache, HAProxy, Ansible and PostgreSQL) when creating a project. It is off by default and only gates creation: a project that already uses one keeps its view.
How many days before a credential expires the warning badge first appears.
The number of columns in the grid, or auto for a responsive layout.
Whether the members of a bundle are grouped under their bundle's card in the grid.
When on, the main grid shows section headings that group the cards by secret type.
When on, which is the default, entries that share a key pool collapse into one card in the grid. The Key Pools tool pane always shows every member.

Keeps the local vault's key in memory after you switch to a remote vault. It is off by default: when off, connecting to a remote clears the local key, so switching back asks for the master password again.
The sort mode last chosen in the grid toolbar.
The last grid view, restored at launch when remember filters is on.

Locks the vault the moment the window is hidden, by switching windows or minimising. It is off by default, because switching windows used to end your session; the inactivity timer already covers walking away.
Whether secret values are masked with dots when the cards load.

Whether profile metadata is written as # comments or as variables. Comments are the default, because a .env is loaded into a process and six extra variables per credential in every container is a cost nobody asked for by pressing Copy.
Whether the first-run wizard has been shown. It is set when the wizard is finished or skipped, and Settings has a button to run it again on purpose.
The ordered list of activity-bar panel ids. It controls the display order and which panels are visible.
The search strings you used lately, newest first, up to a fixed maximum.
Whether the last grid view is restored when the app starts.
The settings of a remote vault server, in the older single-remote form.
The saved connections to remote vault servers.
Whether a warning badge is shown on secrets that are close to expiring.
Whether the sidebar is collapsed, the state toggled with Ctrl-B.
The ordered list of sidebar sections to show. A section that is not in the list is hidden.

The sidebar width in pixels, or 0 for the stylesheet default. It is kept as a number, not a CSS string, so a corrupt settings blob cannot inject CSS, and it is clamped to the bounds the drag handle uses.
The colour theme. System follows the operating system's preference.
Your own order for the Group by type headings. Types you do not list follow the built-in order.
